### Subsection 3 of 12 - Topic 3

Baseline measurements are taken before any active intervention so that subsequent changes can be attributed with confidence. We document three reference points: the steady state before any perturbation, the response to a benign control, and the response to a known stimulus whose effect is already well characterized in the literature. These three together give us a calibration curve against which new results can be checked. ### Subsection 5 of 12 - Topic 5

Trade-offs are surfaced explicitly because no single configuration dominates every axis. Faster procedures sacrifice precision; cheaper procedures sacrifice reliability; more invasive procedures produce richer data but constrain the population from which subjects can be drawn. The remainder of this subsection enumerates the most consequential trade-offs and indicates the regime in which each becomes binding. ### Subsection 6 of 12 - Topic 6

Outcome captures the observed result plus the conditions under which it holds. We avoid the temptation to over-generalize: the effect is present in our sample, plausible in adjacent populations, and untested in regimes far from ours. The goal is to enable informed extrapolation rather than to encourage overclaiming. Recovery describes how to return to a usable state after a partial failure. ### Subsection 10 of 12 - Topic 10

Variance characterizes the spread of outcomes across runs. A procedure that produces a consistent result is easier to trust than one that produces a wide range of similar-but-different results; we report both the central tendency and the spread so the reader can judge whether the spread is acceptable for their purpose.
